# Case study: SOC alert triage {#sec-ch25}

```{python}
#| include: false
import numpy as np
from jevkit import ops
```

Every chapter so far has taken one piece of Kestrel's problem and looked at it closely. Calibration here, a threshold there, an agent, a pattern.

This chapter puts the pieces back together and runs the whole thing, the way a real team would. We'll meet the SOC as it was before any of this. We'll design the new system and run it in silence for a week before trusting it. Then we'll switch it on, and in the week after, a phishing campaign arrives.

*"Is this where it all works perfectly?"*

No. That's the point of a case study. You'll see where it helps a lot, where it helps less than you'd hope, and the one assumption that turned out to matter most.

::: {.goals}
- Describe a SOC's triage before a decision layer, and measure what it quietly misses.
- Assemble the system from the book's pieces, and name which chapter each piece comes from.
- Run a new decision system in shadow mode before it acts, and read what shadow mode shows.
- See why the order of a review queue matters as much as its size.
- Handle a campaign that breaks the base rate, with monitoring, recalibration and overtime.
:::

## Before: the queue

Kestrel's SOC gets about {{< num ch21 live_per_day int >}} alerts a day. Six analysts can each clear about forty, so a day's capacity is {{< num ch25 capacity int >}}. Before this project, every alert joined one queue. The alerts that the senior analyst's rules flagged went to the front; everything else was first come, first served. Whatever nobody reached within a day aged out and was closed without anyone looking.

That's a very ordinary way to run a SOC. It's also invisible in a particular way: nobody ever sees the alerts that age out, so nobody knows how many of them were real.

In our synthetic week, we do know. About {{< num ch25 old.threats_unseen_per_day f1 >}} real threats a day were never seen by anyone.

![Where each day's alerts go, and where the real threats go, before and after. Before, most alerts aged out of the queue unseen, and so did a large share of real threats. After, most alerts are closed by the policy on purpose, and most real threats are queued or paged.](/figures/ch25/routes.pdf){#fig-routes}

The left half of @fig-routes looks similar before and after: most alerts get closed without a person either way. The right half is the difference. Before, alerts were closed by *running out of time*, with no regard for which ones mattered. After, they're closed by a *decision*, and the real threats mostly end up in front of a person.

## The system

![The whole system, with the chapter each piece comes from. Alerts go to Jev as typed questions, the answers are calibrated, the policy routes each alert, and people see the queue and the pages. The LLM writes only for them. Everything is logged and monitored, and labels from reviews and a random audit feed back into calibration.](/figures/ch25/system.pdf){#fig-system}

There's nothing in @fig-system you haven't built. The alert's fields go to Jev as three typed questions (Chapter 17). Platt scaling, fitted on three weeks of history, makes the probabilities honest at Kestrel (Chapters 4 and 18). The three-zone policy, with its lines set by cost and capacity, routes each alert (Chapter 21). The LLM writes the case note for the queue and the message for the page, and nothing else (Chapters 22 and 24). And every decision is logged with its inputs, answers and policy version.

[[AUTHOR STORY: what the first design review of a system like this looked like, and the question from a stakeholder you didn't expect]]

## A week in the shadows

You don't switch a system like this on and hope. You run it in **shadow mode**: it sees every alert and records what it *would* have done, while the analysts carry on exactly as before. Nothing it decides touches anything.

::: {.tryit lab="ch25"}
```{python}
r = ops.before_after()
y, zone = r["y"].astype(bool), r["new"][0]
for z in ("act", "review", "escalate"):
    print(f"{z:>9}: {((zone == z) & y).sum() / 7:4.1f} threats/day")
```
:::

At the end of the shadow week, you put what it would have done next to what turned out to be true.

![Shadow mode's verdict, per day of the live week. Each cell counts alerts by what the system would have done and what they turned out to be. The red cell is the one to argue about: real threats it would have closed on its own.](/figures/ch25/shadow.pdf){#fig-shadow}

The meeting after a shadow week is mostly about one cell, the red one in @fig-shadow: about {{< num ch25 new_threats_closed_per_day f1 >}} real threats a day that the system would have auto-closed. That sounds bad until you compare it with the old queue, which let {{< num ch25 old.threats_unseen_per_day f1 >}} a day age out. It's also exactly the number Chapter 21 predicted before the week began. That's worth saying out loud in the meeting. A system whose mistakes match its own forecast is one you can plan around.

The team's decision was to switch it on, with two conditions from Chapter 21: a random audit of 3% of auto-closed alerts, and a fail-safe that sends an alert to review whenever a call fails.

## Order matters as much as size

Here's a detail that took me by surprise when I ran the numbers.

The new review queue is sorted by probability: the alerts most likely to be real are looked at first. What if we'd kept the old habit of first come, first served, with the same alerts in the same queue?

The median real threat in the review queue would wait about {{< num ch25 fifo_wait int >}} minutes. Sorted by probability, it waits about {{< num ch25 prio_wait int >}}.

Same analysts. Same alerts. Same queue. The only change is the order.

![How long it takes for a real threat to reach a person. Before, rule-flagged threats were seen quickly and the rest waited up to a day or were never seen. After, pages reach someone in about fifteen minutes and the queue takes the likeliest threats first.](/figures/ch25/time-to-human.pdf){#fig-time-to-human}

@fig-time-to-human shows the whole distribution. The old way wasn't slow for everything. Rule-flagged threats jumped the queue and were seen within minutes. Its problem was the long flat stretch: threats the rules didn't flag waited behind everything else, and many never got a turn. After the change, {{< num ch25 new.threats_within_hour_share pct >}} of real threats reach a person within an hour, against {{< num ch25 old.threats_within_hour_share pct >}} before.

::: {.keyidea}
A probability doesn't only decide *whether* a person looks. It decides *what they look at first*. Ordering the queue is often the cheapest improvement available.
:::

## The campaign

The system went live. Then a phishing campaign started.

Link alerts fired three times as often as usual, and far more of them were real. Chapter 21 used this same week to show how drift looks on a monitoring dashboard. Here's what it did to the operation.

![The campaign week, day by day, with and without a response on day 3. Left: alerts sent to review, against the team's capacity. Right: real threats never seen by a person, added up over the week. Recalibrating link alerts and adding overtime helped, but it didn't make the problem go away.](/figures/ch25/campaign.pdf){#fig-campaign}

On day 1 the review queue was already over capacity, peaking at {{< num ch25 camp_peak_reviews int >}} alerts a day against {{< num ch25 capacity int >}}. And the probabilities were now too low for link alerts, because they'd been calibrated on weeks when those alerts were mostly harmless. The monitoring from Chapter 21 caught both on day 2: the queue was over its line, and the reviewers were confirming far more link alerts than predicted.

On day 3 the team responded in two ways. They re-estimated the base rate for link alerts from what reviewers had confirmed so far, and adjusted those probabilities with the prior-shift correction from Chapter 18. And they approved overtime: two extra analysts' worth of reviews a day.

It helped. Over the week, the real threats never seen by a person fell from about {{< num ch25 camp_missed_base int >}} to about {{< num ch25 camp_missed_resp int >}} (@fig-campaign). But look at the left panel: with honest probabilities, the queue grew *past* the overtime capacity. Once the link alerts' probabilities were corrected, far more of them deserved a look than even the enlarged team could give.

That's the uncomfortable truth of the campaign week. Calibration tells you honestly how much work there is. It can't make the work smaller. When the world gets more dangerous, the decision layer's job is to make that visible early and to spend scarce attention on the likeliest threats. The rest is staffing.

## After five weeks

![Kestrel's triage before and after, on the same synthetic live week, with the same six analysts.](/figures/ch25/scorecard.pdf){#fig-scorecard}

@fig-scorecard is the summary I'd put in front of Kestrel's leadership. The analysts looked at about the same number of alerts a day. They weren't working harder. They were looking at different alerts, in a different order, and more real threats reached them, sooner.

One line needs a word of honesty. The *median* wait for a seen threat went up, from about five minutes to fifteen. That's because the old way's seen threats were mostly the rule-flagged ones that jumped the queue, and because I assumed on-call takes fifteen minutes to respond to a page. The fair comparison is the one above it: the share of all real threats seen within an hour more than doubled.

::: {.breaks}
This whole case study is a simulation on synthetic alerts, with mock Jev and made-up costs, capacities and response times, so treat every number as an illustration of the method. Real SOCs differ in ways it leaves out: analysts aren't interchangeable, alerts arrive in bursts, and some real threats are caught later by other defences. Shadow mode is only as good as the labels you compare against, and labels for alerts nobody reviewed are exactly the ones you don't have; that's why the random audit matters. And the campaign response used labels from the first two days, which means the system was wrong for two days before anyone could fix it.
:::

::: {.threshold}
During the campaign, Kestrel can afford overtime for two more analysts, or it can tell the policy to auto-close more link alerts to keep the queue at capacity. A missed threat costs about \$10,000; an analyst-day of overtime costs about \$600. The corrected probabilities say the extra reviews would find roughly one real threat for every six alerts. Which would you choose?

(Each extra analyst clears about 40 alerts a day, which at one threat in six finds about 6 or 7 real threats worth around \$65,000. That's roughly a hundred times the cost of the overtime. Staff up, and keep the lines honest: shrinking the queue by closing likely threats just moves the cost to where nobody sees it.)
:::

::: {.bookquote by="W. Edwards Deming, attributed"}
A bad system will beat a good person every time.
:::

Deming said something like this often, in talks and seminars [[VERIFY]]. Kestrel's analysts were never the problem. The old queue decided what they saw by accident. The new one decides on purpose.

## Where we are

Kestrel's SOC used to decide by running out of time: whatever nobody reached aged out, and a large share of real threats went with it. We assembled the new system from pieces built across the book and ran it in shadow mode. Its mistakes matched its own forecast, so the team switched it on. With the same six analysts, more real threats reached a person, and they got there faster. The cheapest part of that gain came from putting the likeliest threats first. Then a phishing campaign arrived. Recalibration and overtime reduced the damage, and they also showed plainly how much more work the world had created.
